course.title: Academic Research and Information Literacy
course.description: An applied introduction to academic inquiry, source evaluation, strategic searching, evidence synthesis, research ethics and scholarly attribution.

outcomes.text: Formulate focused, researchable questions from broad topics or practical problems.
Evaluate the authority, relevance, currency, evidence and limitations of information sources.
Design and document reproducible search strategies across scholarly and public information environments.
Synthesize evidence from multiple sources into a coherent, appropriately attributed academic argument.
Apply research-integrity, copyright, citation and responsible-AI principles to academic work.

lessons.title: From topic to research problem
objectives: Distinguish a topic, problem, question and claim
Narrow a broad interest into a researchable scope
lessons.teaching_material: Academic research begins with a problem that can be investigated rather than a topic that can merely be described. A useful research problem identifies a gap, tension, uncertainty or decision. Scope is controlled by population, place, period, phenomenon and available evidence. Strong questions are answerable with evidence, sufficiently narrow for the assignment, and open enough to require analysis rather than a yes/no response.
lessons.activity: Choose a broad topic, write three progressively narrower questions, then justify which question is most feasible within a six-week study window.

self_check.q: Why is 'artificial intelligence' not yet a research question?
self_check.a: It names a broad topic but does not identify a bounded problem, population, relationship or evidence need.

self_check.q: What makes a question researchable?
self_check.a: It can be investigated with accessible evidence, has a defined scope and requires analysis rather than unsupported opinion.

lessons.title: Claims, evidence and uncertainty
lessons.teaching_material: A claim is a statement that requires support; evidence is the information used to justify it. Evidence does not automatically prove a claim: its strength depends on relevance, quality, method and alternative explanations. Academic writing should match confidence to evidence. Terms such as suggests, is associated with, estimates and under these conditions often communicate evidence more accurately than absolute language such as proves or always.
lessons.activity: Take five claims from a news article or report and classify each as descriptive, causal, predictive or normative. List what evidence would be needed to support each claim.

self_check.q: Can a correlation alone establish causation?
self_check.a: No. Causal inference requires stronger design or evidence that addresses confounding and alternative explanations.

self_check.q: Why should confidence language vary?
self_check.a: Because the wording should reflect the strength, scope and uncertainty of the available evidence.

lessons.title: Authority is contextual
objectives: Distinguish primary, secondary and tertiary sources
lessons.teaching_material: Authority is not a permanent label attached to a source. It depends on the question being asked, the creator's expertise, the publication process, evidence transparency and possible conflicts of interest. A government statistical release may be authoritative for an official count, while a peer-reviewed study may be stronger for testing an explanatory relationship. Primary sources provide original evidence; secondary sources interpret or analyze it; tertiary sources organize established knowledge.
lessons.activity: For one research question, identify one primary, one secondary and one tertiary source. Explain what each can and cannot establish.

self_check.q: Is a peer-reviewed article always the best source?
self_check.a: No. Suitability depends on the information need; official data, legislation or original records may be more appropriate for some questions.

self_check.q: What is a conflict of interest?
self_check.a: A relationship or incentive that could influence, or appear to influence, judgement, interpretation or reporting.

lessons.title: Evaluating credibility and evidence quality
lessons.teaching_material: Source evaluation should examine authorship, purpose, evidence, method, date, transparency, corroboration and limitations. Popularity, polished design and search ranking are not evidence of reliability. Watch for cherry-picked statistics, missing denominators, unrepresentative samples, causal claims from observational data, quotations detached from context and references that do not support the stated claim. Verification improves when important claims can be traced to original evidence and independently corroborated.
lessons.activity: Audit two conflicting sources on the same claim using a table with columns for author, purpose, evidence, method, limitations, funding and corroboration.

self_check.q: Why is search ranking not a credibility measure?
self_check.a: Ranking reflects platform relevance and other signals, not a scholarly judgement that the information is true.

self_check.q: What does corroboration add?
self_check.a: It checks whether independent evidence supports the same material claim and reduces reliance on a single source.

lessons.title: Search concepts, keywords and databases
objectives: Use Boolean and phrase searching appropriately
lessons.teaching_material: Efficient searching begins by decomposing a research question into its major concepts. Each concept can have synonyms, acronyms, spelling variants and controlled vocabulary. Boolean AND narrows by requiring concepts, OR broadens within a concept, and quotation marks can preserve exact phrases where supported. Search strategies should be adapted to each database rather than copied blindly because indexing, fields and syntax differ.
lessons.activity: Build a search matrix for a research question with at least three concepts and four alternative terms per concept. Run two variants and record how the result set changes.

self_check.q: What does OR usually do in a search?
self_check.a: It broadens retrieval by accepting alternative terms for the same or related concept.

self_check.q: Why keep a search record?
self_check.a: It makes the process reproducible and helps explain why sources were included or missed.

lessons.title: Citation chasing and evidence trails
objectives: Use backward and forward citation searching
lessons.teaching_material: Keyword searching is only one discovery route. Backward citation chasing examines the references used by a relevant source; forward citation searching identifies later work that cites it. Together they reveal intellectual lineages, replications, critiques and updates. A research log should record database, date, search string, filters, promising sources and exclusion reasons so the search can be reproduced or improved later.
lessons.activity: Select one strong source, trace two references backward and two citations forward, then draw a small evidence network showing how the sources relate.

self_check.q: What can forward citation searching reveal?
self_check.a: Later studies that extend, replicate, critique or apply the earlier work.

self_check.q: What is the purpose of an exclusion reason?
self_check.a: It makes selection decisions transparent and reduces arbitrary source picking.

lessons.title: Paraphrase, quotation and synthesis
objectives: Synthesize multiple sources around an idea
lessons.teaching_material: Paraphrasing means restating an idea accurately in a genuinely new structure and wording while preserving attribution. Replacing a few words in the source sentence is patchwriting, not an independent paraphrase. Synthesis goes further: it organizes multiple sources around a question, pattern or disagreement instead of summarizing sources one at a time. Direct quotation should be selective and used when the original wording itself matters.
lessons.activity: Write a 180-word synthesis using three short source summaries. Organize by agreement/disagreement rather than by author and attach citations to the specific claims they support.

self_check.q: Does paraphrased material require citation?
self_check.a: Yes. Rewording does not transfer ownership of the underlying idea or evidence.

self_check.q: What distinguishes synthesis from a list of summaries?
self_check.a: Synthesis integrates sources around concepts, relationships, patterns or disagreements.

lessons.title: Citation integrity, copyright and responsible AI
objectives: Use AI without misrepresenting authorship or evidence
lessons.teaching_material: Citation integrity requires that factual or scholarly claims can be traced to sources and that listed references are actually used. A citation must support the nearby claim; merely attaching a plausible reference is not enough. Copyright governs reuse of protected expression, while citation concerns attribution and scholarly traceability. When AI tools are permitted, students remain responsible for verifying claims, sources, quotations, calculations and originality. AI output is not evidence simply because it sounds authoritative.
lessons.activity: Audit a short AI-assisted draft. Verify every factual claim against a primary or scholarly source, remove unsupported references and document where AI materially contributed.

self_check.q: Can a fabricated AI citation be kept if the claim is true?
self_check.a: No. A reference must correspond to a real source that actually supports the claim.

self_check.q: Does citation permission automatically permit copying large passages?
self_check.a: No. Attribution and copyright permission are separate issues.

modules.title: Research Design, Ethics and Evidence Synthesis

lessons.title: Matching questions to methods
objectives: Match common research questions to suitable methods
lessons.teaching_material: Research design follows the question. Descriptive questions may use observation, surveys or descriptive datasets; relationship questions may use correlational or comparative designs; causal questions require designs capable of addressing alternative explanations; meaning and experience questions may require qualitative methods. No method is universally superior. The researcher must justify why a design can answer the stated question and acknowledge what it cannot establish.
lessons.activity: For four research questions, select a plausible design, identify the unit of analysis, specify the evidence needed and state one major limitation.

self_check.q: Why should method follow the question?
self_check.a: Because different questions require different kinds of evidence and support different levels of inference.

self_check.q: What is a unit of analysis?
self_check.a: The entity about which observations are made and conclusions are drawn, such as people, firms, countries or documents.

lessons.title: Research ethics and transparent synthesis
objectives: Build an evidence matrix for synthesis
lessons.teaching_material: Ethical research protects participants, respects consent and confidentiality, minimizes harm, avoids deception unless justified and reviewed, and reports findings honestly. Secondary research also has ethical obligations: do not distort a source, hide contradictory findings or present selective evidence as consensus. An evidence matrix records source, question, method, sample, key finding, limitation and relevance, making synthesis more systematic and exposing where evidence is thin or conflicting.
lessons.activity: Build an evidence matrix for six sources and write a short conclusion that explicitly includes one limitation and one contradictory finding.

self_check.q: Can literature review work have ethical problems even without human participants?
self_check.a: Yes. Misrepresentation, selective reporting, plagiarism and fabricated citations are research-integrity failures.

self_check.q: Why record limitations in an evidence matrix?
self_check.a: They affect how strongly each source should influence the final synthesis.

lessons.title: From evidence matrix to argument
objectives: Develop a defensible thesis from evidence
lessons.teaching_material: A defensible thesis is a conclusion that follows from the evidence while acknowledging uncertainty and boundaries. Analytical paragraphs normally begin with a claim, present relevant evidence, explain how the evidence bears on the claim, and connect the reasoning to the wider argument. Counterevidence should be addressed rather than hidden. The quality of an argument depends less on the number of references than on whether the sources are relevant, credible and correctly interpreted.
lessons.activity: Convert an evidence matrix into a one-page argument map containing thesis, three supporting claims, evidence for each claim, counterevidence and limitations.

self_check.q: What makes a thesis defensible?
self_check.a: It is supported by the available evidence, bounded to what that evidence can justify and responsive to important counterevidence.

self_check.q: Why is source count alone a poor quality measure?
self_check.a: Many weak or irrelevant citations do not compensate for poor evidence or reasoning.

lessons.title: Reproducible mini literature review
lessons.teaching_material: A reproducible mini literature review states its question, describes how evidence was searched and selected, synthesizes findings, identifies limitations and provides a traceable reference list. The final integrity check should confirm that every in-text citation has a matching reference, each reference is actually used, quoted wording is accurate, claims are supported at the stated level of certainty, and AI assistance has not introduced unverifiable content.
lessons.activity: Prepare the course mini-review package: question, search log, source-evaluation table, evidence matrix, 1,500-word synthesis, reference list and integrity checklist.

self_check.q: What makes a review reproducible?
self_check.a: Another reader can understand and substantially repeat the search and selection process from the documented method.

self_check.q: What is the final citation-integrity check?
self_check.a: Verify both directions: every cited source is in the references and every listed reference is actually cited and supports the associated claim.

assessments.title: Source Evaluation Portfolio
assessments.instructions: Evaluate four sources addressing one question, document a reproducible search strategy and justify inclusion/exclusion decisions.

assessments.title: Evidence Synthesis Brief
assessments.instructions: Produce an 800-word evidence synthesis from at least six credible sources, including one area of disagreement or uncertainty.

assessments.title: Mini Literature Review
assessments.instructions: Submit a 1,500-word mini literature review with research question, search log, evidence matrix, synthesis, limitations, references and research-integrity declaration.
